Quick Lesson · Customer Service

Escalating It Up — when Renata can't decide alone

Not every case fits neatly into the policy. When a client is big, angry, or both, Renata has to bring the case to Diego Marques, her manager — and that means explaining what the client said, professionally, without just repeating it word for word.

Renata Lima · Customer Success, Altiva Biosolutions Diego Marques · Regional Operations Director

Customer Success, Altiva Biosolutions
Handles Marcos's complaint and decides when it's time to escalate.
Marcos
Procurement, Frutamax
The frustrated client sending message after message to Renata.
Diego Marques
Regional Operations Director

02Reported Speech: The Full Backshift

Toda vez que você relata o que alguém disse, o verbo dá um passo pra trás no tempo. A tabela abaixo mostra o padrão completo, não só um exemplo solto.

Direct Speech (what they said)Reported Speech (what you say)
Present Simple → Past Simple"I need a refund." She said she needed a refund.
Present Continuous → Past Continuous"I'm waiting for an answer." He said he was waiting for an answer.
Present Perfect → Past Perfect"I have already contacted you twice." She said she had already contacted them twice.
Past Simple → Past Perfect"I sent the email yesterday." He said he had sent the email the day before.
Will → Would"I will cancel my account." She said she would cancel her account.
Can → Could"I can't wait any longer." He said he couldn't wait any longer.
Must → Had to"I must have an answer today." She said she had to have an answer that day.
Time and place words shift too — not just the verb:
today→that day
yesterday→the day before
tomorrow→the next day
this→that
now→then
here→there
The rule in one line: everything moves one step further from "now" — the verb tense, and any word that points to a specific time or place. You're not quoting — you're summarizing from a later point in time.
One more thing before you practice: do you need "that"? No — it's optional after most reporting verbs. "He said that he needed a refund" and "He said he needed a refund" are both correct; dropping it is just more common in speech. What matters more is choosing the right verb:
SAY
No personal object needed — you just say something.
✓ He said he needed a refund.
✗ He said me he needed a refund.
TELL
Always needs a personal object — you tell someone.
✓ He told me he needed a refund.
✗ He told he needed a refund.
Quick test: a person right after the verb ("me," "her," "Diego") means you need tell. No person there? Use say. "Say to someone" exists, but native speakers almost always say tell someone instead.

05When to Actually Escalate

Escalar demais é tão problemático quanto escalar de menos — o vocabulário de saber a diferença.

a judgment call — "Whether to escalate or not is often a judgment call."
err on the side of caution — "When it's a big account, I'd rather err on the side of caution."
use your discretion — "For small requests like this, use your discretion."
warrants escalation — "A minor delay like this doesn't warrant escalation."
escalate prematurely — "Escalating prematurely can make you look like you can't handle routine cases."
a red flag — "A repeat complaint from the same account is a red flag worth escalating."
In Renata's words
"Not every complaint warrants escalation — most of the time, it's a judgment call I can make with my discretion alone. But when I see a red flag like a repeat issue on a big account, I'd rather err on the side of caution than escalate too prematurely — or, worse, not escalate at all."
06Should Renata Escalate? You Decide

Quatro situações reais. Ela deveria resolver sozinha, ou levar pro Diego?

Situation A
A client asks for a small discount on a routine reorder, well within the standard pricing range Renata already has authority over.
Handle it herself. This is squarely within her normal discretion — escalating something this routine would waste Diego's time and make her look unsure of her own role.
Situation B
A major client threatens to post publicly on social media about a recurring product defect if it isn't resolved by end of day.
Escalate to Diego. This carries reputational risk beyond a normal complaint — exactly the kind of red flag that warrants bringing in someone with broader authority.
Situation C
A client asks a simple question about where their shipment currently is in transit.
Handle it herself. A tracking question isn't a judgment call at all — escalating this would be escalating prematurely, for something with zero risk attached.
Situation D
A client's request technically falls outside policy, but the account is worth renewing at a significant value next quarter.
Escalate to Diego. Approving an exception to policy is above her authority by definition — and with real money on the table, this is exactly where erring on the side of caution makes sense.
07The Escalation Email

A mensagem interna que a Renata manda pro Diego antes de responder ao cliente.

Altiva Biosolutions · Internal
To: Diego Marques · From: Renata Lima
Needs Sign-Off
Subject: Escalating — Frutamax account, repeat complaint

Diego, I wanted to loop you in on something tricky before I respond. Marcos from Frutamax claimed the last shipment had never been properly inspected, and mentioned this is the second issue this quarter. He insisted we owed him a full replacement at no cost — but technically, this falls outside our coverage window.

Frutamax renews in Q1, so I didn't want to just say no. Approving an exception like this is above my authority — can I get your sign-off on a one-time goodwill replacement?
08Build the Conversation: Escalating to Diego

Diego faz perguntas. Em cada momento, escolha a frase que a Renata diria.

Diego
"So what's going on with the Frutamax account?"
What does Renata say?
This opens the conversation clearly and professionally — not alarming, not dismissive, just direct.
Diego
"What did the client actually say?"
What does Renata say?
This is reported speech done right — specific, and correctly shifted into the past ("had never been").
Diego
"Is this actually within policy?"
What does Renata say?
Honest about the policy, but also honest about why she's not deciding alone — this is exactly what escalating well sounds like.
Diego
"Okay. What do you recommend?"
What does Renata say?
A clear recommendation, with a reason attached — this shows judgment, not just passing the decision up blindly.

Word bank
said authority pointed out sign-off mentioned judgment call insisted discretion loop in prematurely escalate red flag claimed told warrants flag explained err on the side of caution defer
01 · Escalation Language
"I wanted to ______ you in before responding to the client."
loop in — include someone in the conversation.
02 · Escalation Language
"I need your ______ before I can offer an exception."
sign-off — formal approval.
03 · Escalation Language
"I'm going to ______ this to you, since it's a strategic account."
escalate — raise it up the hierarchy.
04 · Escalation Language
"Approving a full refund is above my ______."
authority — as in "above my authority."
05 · Escalation Language
"On accounts this size, I ______ to you for the final call."
defer — let someone else make the final decision.
06 · Escalation Language
"I wanted to ______ this internally before it becomes a bigger issue."
flag — raise a concern before it grows.
07 · Reported Speech
Client: "I already contacted you twice." → He ______ he had already contacted them twice.
said — the neutral reporting verb.
08 · Reported Speech
Client: "This shipment never arrived." → She ______ the shipment had never arrived.
claimed — used when you're not sure it's fully accurate.
09 · Reported Speech
Diego ______ that the account was too important to lose over this.
pointed out — drew attention to a specific fact.
10 · Reported Speech
The client ______ that he'd been a loyal customer for five years, hoping that would help his case.
mentioned — said casually, in passing.
11 · Reported Speech
Marcos ______ on getting a full replacement, not just a partial credit.
insisted — repeated a demand firmly.
12 · Reported Speech
Renata ______ why the claim technically fell outside the coverage window.
explained — gave reasons or context.
13 · When to Escalate
Whether to escalate or not is often a ______ call, not a fixed rule.
judgment — as in "a judgment call."
14 · When to Escalate
On a big account, Renata would rather ______ on the side of caution.
err — as in "err on the side of caution."
15 · When to Escalate
For small, routine requests, Renata is expected to use her own ______.
discretion — her own judgment, without needing to ask.
16 · When to Escalate
A simple tracking question doesn't ______ escalation at all.
warrant — as in "warrants escalation."
17 · When to Escalate
Escalating too ______ can make you look like you can't handle routine cases.
prematurely — too early, before it's really needed.
18 · When to Escalate
A repeat complaint from the same big account is a ______ worth escalating.
red flag — a warning sign that something bigger might be going on.
19 · Say vs. Tell
He ______ me he needed a refund. (there's a person right after the verb)
told — "tell" always needs a personal object.
20 · Say vs. Tell
She ______ she needed a refund. (no person right after the verb)
said — "say" never takes a direct personal object.
21 · Say vs. Tell
Fix this sentence: "He told he needed help." — what's missing?
me (or her/him/us) — "tell" is never followed directly by the clause without a person first.
22 · Say vs. Tell
Marcos ______ Renata the shipment had been damaged.
told — "Renata" is the personal object right after the verb.
23 · The Optional "That"
True or false: you must always include "that" in reported speech. Type "true" or "false."
false — "that" is optional after most reporting verbs. Both versions are correct.
24 · The Optional "That"
"He said that he needed help" and "He said he needed help" are both ______. (one word: correct, wrong, or optional)
correct — both are fully correct. "That" is optional, not required.
